title: The Interview
teaser: An email at 11 p.m. A job in Cairo. One problem: English.
paragraphs: Nour is twenty-seven. She is an accountant in a small company in Tanta. The salary is low, the office is hot, and her boss shouts a lot. Every night, she looks at jobs on her phone. Every good job says the same thing: English required.

On Thursday, at 11 p.m., she sees an email. It is from Hartwell, a big international company in Cairo. “Dear Nour, thank you for your application. We would like to invite you to an interview on Sunday at 10 a.m.”
Nour reads it three times. Then she reads the last line again. The interview will be in English.

Her heart beats fast. She understands English when she reads it. She can watch a video with subtitles. But when she speaks, her mind goes white. At school, a teacher laughed at her accent once, in front of the whole class. She still remembers his face.
Her little brother, Ziad, sees her phone. “An interview? In English? You?” He laughs and goes back to his game.

Nour closes the door of her room. She opens her notes and writes one sentence in English: Could you say that again, please? She says it out loud, quietly. Then again, a little louder. It sounds strange, but it is her voice.
She practises until 1 a.m. She writes small answers: her name, her job, why she wants to work at Hartwell. She is tired, but for the first time in a long time, she feels something new. Hope.
Then her phone rings. It is a number from London. She answers. “H-hello?” “Hi, is this Nour? This is Emma from Hartwell. I’m so sorry, but can we move your interview… to tomorrow morning?”

to ask someone to come
needed; you must have it
the way someone pronounces a language
to do something again and again to get better
the feeling that something good can happen

title: The Interview
teaser: Her cousin gives her one rule: don’t learn answers. Tell stories.
previously: Nour, an accountant in Tanta, has an interview in English at Hartwell in Cairo. At 1 a.m., Emma from London called about changing the day.

openings.A: “Yes, tomorrow is fine,” Nour says. Then she ends the call and looks at the clock. 1:15 a.m. The interview is at 10. She has nine hours, and three of them are on a train.
openings.B: “Could we keep Sunday, please?” Nour asks. There is a short pause. Then Emma laughs. “Of course. Actually, Sunday is better. Our manager, Mr Adel, can join us then.” Nour ends the call and breathes again. She has two days.

paragraphs: She cannot sleep, so she sends a message to her cousin Mona. Mona works in a bank in Cairo and speaks English every day. To Nour’s surprise, Mona calls her back immediately. “I was awake anyway,” she says. “Tell me everything.”
Nour reads her answers to Mona. They are correct, but they sound like a robot. Mona stops her. “Nour, don’t learn answers by heart. You will forget them in the room. Tell stories.”

“Stories?” “Yes. When they say, ‘Tell me about yourself’, use three parts. The past: what you studied and where you work. The present: what you do every day and what you are good at. The future: why you want this job.”

Nour tries. The past is easy. The present is harder, because her job feels small. Mona helps her. “You check two hundred invoices every month and you find mistakes that other people miss. That is not small. That is a skill.”

After the call, Nour practises in front of the mirror. She looks strange to herself, so she closes her eyes and talks to the wardrobe. Suddenly, someone knocks on her door. It is Ziad. He looks embarrassed.

“I heard you,” he says. “Your English is… good. Do you want me to be the interviewer? I can sound like a manager.” He makes a deep, serious voice. Nour laughs for the first time that night. They practise for an hour.

When Ziad goes to bed, Nour opens her wardrobe to choose her clothes. She takes out her only suit, the dark blue one. She holds it under the light. In the middle of the jacket, there is a big brown stain.

targets.en: now, without waiting
from memory
a paper that shows how much a customer must pay
something you can do well because you learned it
feeling shy or ashamed
a dirty mark that is hard to remove

title: The Interview
teaser: The train stops in the middle of nowhere. The interview doesn’t wait.
previously: Mona taught Nour to answer with stories, and Ziad played the interviewer. Then Nour found a big stain on her only suit.
paragraphs: Nour runs to the kitchen with the jacket. Her mother is already awake, making tea. She looks at the stain, then at her daughter’s face. “Sit down,” she says calmly. “Your grandmother had a trick.” She mixes salt and lemon, rubs it gently with an old toothbrush and washes it with cold water.

Twenty minutes later, the stain is almost gone. Her mother dries it with the hairdryer and irons it. Nour hugs her. “You didn’t ask about the interview,” Nour says. Her mother smiles. “I know you. You will be fine.”

At 6:15, Nour is on the train to Cairo with her notes on her knee. She reads her three parts again: past, present, future. A man next to her is reading an English newspaper. She practises in a very quiet voice, but he notices and smiles. “Good luck,” he says in English. She answers in English too: “Thank you.”

Then, near Banha, the train slows down and stops. Five minutes. Ten minutes. Twenty minutes. People start to complain. A worker walks through the train and says there is a problem with the engine. Nobody knows how long it will take.

Nour looks at her phone. 8:40. If the train does not move soon, she will be late. Her hands are cold. She knows she must call Emma, but she has never made a phone call in English. Her finger stays over the number.

The man with the newspaper sees her face. “Calling is better than not calling,” he says gently. Nour takes a breath and presses the button. “Hello, Emma? This is Nour. I’m so sorry. My train has stopped. I’m running about twenty minutes late.”

“Oh, don’t worry,” says Emma. “Thank you for telling us. Just come when you can.” Nour ends the call and laughs quietly. She did it. The train starts to move. At 10:25, she runs into the Hartwell building, out of breath. The receptionist looks up. “Nour? Mr Adel is waiting for you. He doesn’t like waiting.”

targets.en: a clever way of doing something
to move something hard over a surface
to make clothes smooth with a hot tool
to say you are not happy about something
the part of a machine that makes it move
the person who welcomes visitors at the front desk

phrase.en: I’m so sorry, I’m running about twenty minutes late.
phrase.ar: آسف جدًا، هتأخر حوالي عشرين دقيقة.

title: The Interview
teaser: The question she feared most: “Tell us about a mistake you made.”
previously: Nour’s train stopped near Banha, and she made her first phone call in English to say she was late. Now Mr Adel is waiting, and he doesn’t like waiting.
paragraphs: Mr Adel is about fifty, with grey hair and very serious glasses. He is Egyptian, but he speaks only English in the interview. On a big screen on the wall, Emma smiles and waves from London. “Welcome, Nour. Shall we start?”

“Tell me about yourself,” says Mr Adel. Nour’s mind goes white for one second. Then she remembers: past, present, future. She talks about her studies in Tanta, her four years at the company, the two hundred invoices every month. Her voice shakes a little at first, but then it gets stronger. Mr Adel writes something in his notebook.
Then Emma asks a question. She speaks very fast, with a British accent, and Nour understands only three words: “team”, “pressure” and “deadline”. Her heart jumps. The room is silent.

Then she remembers her sentence, the first one she wrote that night. “I’m sorry,” she says. “Could you say that again, please?” Emma smiles and asks again, more slowly: “How do you work under pressure, when the deadline is very close?”

Now Nour understands, and she has a story. At the end of every month, her boss gives her the invoices late, and she has two days for a week of work. She makes a list, she starts with the biggest clients, and she checks everything twice. Mr Adel nods.
The interview goes well. Nour starts to relax. Then Mr Adel puts down his pen and looks at her. “Last question,” he says. “Tell us about a big mistake you made at work.”

Nour freezes, but not because of English this time. She remembers a real mistake: last year, she sent a client an invoice with an extra zero. Fifty thousand pounds instead of five thousand. Her boss shouted for a week. She has never told anyone how bad she felt.

targets.en: not joking or smiling
to move quickly because of fear or cold
the feeling of having too much to do
the last time to finish something
to become calm
a person or company that pays for a service

title: The Interview
teaser: The interview is over. Now the hardest part: waiting.
previously: The interview went well, until Mr Adel asked about a big mistake. Nour remembered the invoice with an extra zero: fifty thousand instead of five thousand.

openings.A: Nour takes a breath and tells the truth. The extra zero, the angry client, her boss shouting. Then she tells the end of the story: she called the client herself, apologised, and made a new checklist that the whole office uses now. Mr Adel takes off his glasses. For the first time, he smiles.
openings.B: “I’m a perfectionist,” Nour says. “I don’t really make mistakes.” Emma tilts her head. “Everyone makes mistakes, Nour. Can you give us one example?” Nour’s face is hot. So she tells the truth: the extra zero, the angry client, and the checklist she made after it. Mr Adel takes off his glasses and nods slowly.

paragraphs: “Thank you, Nour,” says Emma. “We will be in touch soon.” Nour stands up, shakes Mr Adel’s hand, and walks out of the building. On the street, the Cairo traffic is loud and hot. She feels light, like after an exam.

On the train home, she writes an email to Emma. Mona told her to do this. It is short and polite: “Thank you for your time today. I enjoyed our conversation, and I look forward to hearing from you.” She reads it ten times before she presses Send.

Then the waiting starts. Sunday, nothing. Monday, nothing. On Tuesday, she goes back to her old office. Her boss shouts because the printer is broken, as if it is her fault. She smiles politely and thinks: maybe soon I won’t be here.

Wednesday, nothing. Thursday, nothing. Nour checks her email every ten minutes, then every five minutes. Ziad stops making jokes about it. Her mother makes her favourite food, molokhia, without saying why.

On Friday morning, Nour is drinking tea on the balcony when her phone buzzes. A new email. From: Hartwell. Subject: Your application. Her finger stops above the screen. Good news or bad news? She cannot open it.

title: The Interview
teaser: Not a yes. Not a no. Something in between.
previously: After the interview, Nour waited a whole week. On Friday morning, an email from Hartwell arrived, and she was afraid to open it.
paragraphs: Ziad comes onto the balcony and sees her face. “Open it,” he says. “If it’s bad, I will eat all the molokhia so you can be sad in peace.” Nour laughs, and she opens it.

“Dear Nour, thank you for interviewing with us. We have decided to offer the accountant position to a candidate with more experience.” Her stomach drops. She stops reading. Ziad takes the phone gently from her hand and reads the rest out loud, slowly.

“However, the team was very impressed with your honesty and your attention to detail. We would like to offer you a different role: Junior Accountant, for a three-month trial, starting in two weeks. The role includes English training.”

Nour reads it again herself. It is not the job she wanted. The salary is only a little higher than now, and Cairo is expensive. She would need to rent a room, maybe share a flat with strangers. But it is Hartwell. It is a door.
At lunch, she tells the family. Her mother is worried. “Cairo, alone? And only three months?” Ziad thinks it is cool. Her father says nothing. He eats slowly and looks at his plate.

After lunch, Nour writes to Emma. She does not want to say yes too fast, and she does not want to say no. Mona helps her with one sentence: “Thank you so much for this offer. Could I have a day to think about it?” Emma answers in five minutes: “Of course. Take your time.”

That evening, Nour is in her room when her father knocks on the door. He has never done that before. He stands in the doorway, holding an old brown envelope. “Nour,” he says quietly, “come and sit with me. I need to tell you something.”

title: The Interview
teaser: Thirty years ago, her father got a letter. He never opened the door.
previously: Hartwell offered Nour a three-month trial job in Cairo. She asked for a day to think. Then her father came to her room with an old brown envelope.
paragraphs: Her father sits on the edge of the bed. He opens the envelope and takes out a yellow letter. It is in English, typed on an old machine. The date at the top is 1994.
“I was twenty-six,” he says. “A company in Kuwait offered me a job. Good money. A future. I read this letter a hundred times.” He touches the paper softly. “And I said no.”

“Why?” Nour asks. Her father is quiet for a moment. “Because I was afraid. Afraid of the English, afraid to be alone, afraid to fail. I told everyone it was because of my mother. But the truth is, I was afraid.”
Nour has never heard her father talk like this. He always seemed strong and sure. Now he looks like a young man in an old photo.

“I have a good life,” he continues. “I have you, your brother, your mother. I am not sad every day. But sometimes, at night, I think about this letter. I think: what if?” He puts the letter in her hands. “I don’t want you to have an envelope like this.”
Nour cannot speak. Her eyes are full. Her father stands up and smiles. “Go to Cairo,” he says. “If it doesn’t work, you come home. Your room will wait for you. But go.”

After he leaves, Nour opens the email from Hartwell again. The offer is good, but the salary is small for Cairo. Mona said that sometimes you can ask for more, politely. But maybe they will be angry. Maybe they will take the offer back. Nour looks at the yellow letter on her bed. Then she starts to type.

title: The Interview
teaser: Day one. She still doesn’t understand everything. She speaks anyway.
previously: Nour’s father told her about the job in Kuwait he refused because of fear, and told her to go. Nour answered Hartwell.

openings.A: Nour accepted the offer the same night. Two weeks later, she shares a small flat in Dokki with a nurse from Assiut, and she walks to the Hartwell building at 8:30 in her blue suit.
openings.B: Nour accepted, and politely asked about the salary. Her heart beat fast for a whole day. Then Emma answered: “We can add ten percent and help with your first month of rent.” Two weeks later, Nour walks to the Hartwell building at 8:30 in her blue suit.

paragraphs: At nine o’clock, there is a team meeting. Ten people sit around a long table. Some are Egyptian, one is from India, and Emma is there in person, visiting from London for a week. Everyone speaks English, fast, with jokes Nour doesn’t understand.

For the first twenty minutes, she says nothing. She understands maybe half. Her old fear comes back: what if they ask me something? What if my accent is strange? Then Mr Adel says, “Nour, you checked the March invoices. Anything interesting?”

Everyone looks at her. Her mind goes white for one second, like on the first night. Then she hears her own voice. “I’m sorry, could you say that again, please?” Mr Adel repeats the question, slowly. And Nour answers. She found three invoices with the wrong tax number. Small mistakes, but expensive ones.

The room is quiet. Then a man from the finance team, Karim, laughs. “Three? I checked them last month and found nothing.” Emma writes something down. Mr Adel nods. “Good. Show Karim after the meeting.”

At lunch, a woman from Alexandria called Sara sits next to her. “Your first day, right? I was so scared on my first day that I said ‘good night’ to the CEO at ten in the morning.” Nour laughs so much she almost drops her sandwich.
That evening, in her small room in Dokki, Nour calls home. Her mother asks if she ate. Ziad asks if she met anyone famous. Her father asks only one question: “Are you glad you went?”
Nour looks out of the window at the lights of Cairo. She thinks of the girl who wrote one sentence in her notes at 11 p.m., one month ago. “Yes, Baba,” she says. “I’m glad I went.”
